title: The Mughals
hookLine: Babur, Akbar and their successors rule much of South Asia

cards: A king is writing his diary, and he is homesick. He has just won a great battle and taken Delhi and Agra: treasure, elephants, a new country. And what does he complain about?
The melons. In his own memoir, he grumbles that his new land has no good melons and grapes, no cold running water, no proper gardens laid out in order.
He misses the orchards of the valley where he grew up, far to the north in Central Asia. So, the memoir says, he soon starts digging channels and planting a garden.
His name was Babur, and his family would rule much of South Asia. Today: the Mughals.

teach.b: Babur was a descendant of Timur, the same family line as Ulugh Beg of Samarkand. He lost his own small kingdom in Central Asia, came south through Kabul, and won his way into India.
His memoir, written in his Turkic mother tongue, is frank: battles, friendships, regrets, his drinking and his giving it up, and gardens everywhere.
The Mughal garden became a signature: beds divided by water channels, with a pool or a pavilion at the center.

The Qur'an pictures paradise as gardens with water. In Pickthall's translation: "Gardens underneath which rivers flow." Many historians read a walled Mughal garden with running water as a small picture of that promise.
He built a new city at Fatehpur Sikri, and in it a hall where he invited scholars to debate: Sunni and Shi'a Muslims, Hindus, Jains, Zoroastrians, and Jesuit priests from Portuguese Goa.

He listened, asked questions, and let them argue in front of him. Some Muslim scholars of his court admired this, and some objected strongly, and historians still argue about what Akbar himself came to believe.

After Akbar came his son Jahangir, then Shah Jahan, then Aurangzeb, each with his own story, and the empire's courts filled with Persian poetry, painting, music and buildings of red sandstone and white marble.
Babur's homesick garden had grown into an empire.

how: Mughal mosques, tombs and gardens in India and Pakistan, such as the Jama Masjid in Delhi and the Badshahi Mosque in Lahore, are still places of prayer and visiting today.

games.q: you're Babur. you've just won Delhi and Agra, and you miss the orchards of home. what do you do first?
o: go back north to the valley.
dig water channels and plant a garden.
games.why: his memoir says he started digging channels and planting a garden. the Mughal garden, with water at its center, became a signature.

practice: Choose one Mughal city: Agra with its red fort by the river, Delhi with its great mosque, Lahore with its gardens, or Fatehpur Sikri, Akbar's city of debate.

Picture yourself walking in, the way Babur walked into a new land, and notice what you'd look for first: water, a garden, a mosque, a market. If you pray, you can remember the people who prayed there.

wordCard.voice: The Mughals. The dynasty of Babur and Akbar and their successors, who ruled much of South Asia and filled it with gardens, poetry and marble. Today's word.

orig.note: Persian and Urdu: Mughal, the name for the dynasty, usually linked to the word for Mongol.

carryVoice: Your line: he missed the melons. Homesickness, planted in the ground as a garden. See you tomorrow.
